target_customer: Individuals who want end-of-life brain or whole-body preservation for possible future revival, in jurisdictions with medical aid in dying
problem: Conventional death destroys brain structure; Nectome claims to preserve synapses and cells so long-term memories could in principle survive.
business_model: Fee-for-service preservation procedure with refundable deposits, plus research funded by grants

founders.name: Aurelia Song
founders.background_notes: YC page lists her as the sole founder and says she studied old-school AI and was Marvin Minsky's last student. She leads a 2026 Nectome preprint per search summary.

founders.name: Robert McIntyre
founders.background_notes: Named co-founder with Michael McCanna in 2018 press coverage (search summary); not on the YC page. The relationship to the YC page founder is not established here.

founders.name: Michael McCanna
founders.background_notes: Named in 2018 press coverage via search summary; not on the YC page.

investors: U.S. National Institute of Mental Health

competitors.name: Alcor Life Extension Foundation
competitors.what: Cryonics provider using vitrification without chemical fixation
competitors.traction_then: Roughly 1,000 members a decade before 2026 per one source; about 250 people preserved across Alcor and CI over 50 years

competitors.name: Cryonics Institute
competitors.traction_then: Whole body from about 28,000 dollars per one source, date not stated

technical_complexity.rationale: Fixing and preserving whole brains at synapse level, with perfusion timing windows of about 12 to 14 minutes, was research-grade; revival is not possible today.

defensibility.rationale: Won the Brain Preservation Foundation 80,000 dollar prize in March 2018 for a pig brain protocol, but the technique is published and the service has legal and trust constraints.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No larger player pursued the same wedge; cryonics providers kept a different method. MIT cut ties with the company in April 2018 after criticism.

market_need_then: Interest from early depositors: a refundable 10,000 dollar deposit program drew sign-ups in March 2018, including a reported high profile depositor, but demand for fatal preservation was niche.

identity.voice_and_tone: Scientific and sober, with a company Substack publishing long explanatory essays

branding.brand_signature: Direct, controversial pitch of fatal preservation that made headlines in 2018
branding.community_and_virality: Heavy 2018 press (MIT Technology Review, Fortune, Vice) and ongoing discussion on LessWrong and a company Substack.

brand_strength.rationale: High press visibility and a distinctive name, though visibility was driven by controversy, and the name's link to connectome is only a plausible inference not a sourced origin.

outcome_analysis: Nectome is still active. It won a prize for pig brain preservation in March 2018, then lost its MIT collaboration in April 2018 after criticism of the fatal uploading pitch, and reported little venture funding (about 120,000 dollars of YC money plus a grant). By 2026 it published a whole pig brain preservation preprint compatible with assisted death, indicating a slow research-led path with niche demand and legal limits.
notes: Founder conflict: YC page lists Aurelia Song only; 2018 press names Robert McIntyre and Michael McCanna as co-founders; the sources opened do not reconcile these. Most press pages (MIT Technology Review, LiveScience body) were not readable, so details come from search summaries. The 960,000 dollar NIMH grant and about 1 million total funding are from search summaries of 2018 coverage; a later profile says roughly 120,000 dollars raised through pre-seed and seed. MIT subcontract about 300,000 dollars. Total reported funding conflicts; funding unverified beyond the grant.
